title: Unit final: exhaustive search and DP
sub: Recognize search or DP from the statement, predict a coin table without a one, find the bug in a 0/1 knapsack, explain out loud
cards/0/q: New problems. Match the statement with the technique.
cards/0/pairs/0/0: All letter words that can be typed with phone digits
cards/0/pairs/0/1: A decision tree: each digit gets its letters
cards/0/pairs/1/0: Can the array be split into two parts with equal sums
cards/0/pairs/2/1: LCS of the string and its reverse
cards/0/pairs/3/0: All valid bracket strings of n pairs
cards/0/pairs/3/1: Pruning: “)” only while fewer are closed than open
cards/0/pairs/4/0: Maximum money without robbing two adjacent houses
cards/1/q: A game has 20 items, each with a weight and a value up to 10⁹, and a backpack capacity up to 10⁹ as well. You need the maximum value of a set that fits. How do you solve it?
cards/1/options/1: 0/1 knapsack over capacity: dp with 10⁹ + 1 cells
cards/1/options/2: Greedy: take items by decreasing value per unit of weight
cards/1/explain: A table over capacity costs O(n·W) = 2·10¹⁰ operations and about 8 GB of memory (value sums up to 2·10¹⁰ need a long) — that is not a solution. But there are only 20 items, and enumerating every set with a mask is about 2·10⁷ steps, a fraction of a second. Which one is cheap — n or W — is decided by the limits.
cards/1/wrong/1: O(n·W) depends on the magnitude of the capacity, not on the number of items: with W = 10⁹ that is 2·10¹⁰ operations and gigabytes of memory — a thousand times slower than enumerating masks.
cards/1/wrong/2: Greedy by value per weight is correct only for the “fractional” knapsack, where an item can be cut. Here an item is taken whole, and greedy fails, as with coins 1, 3, 4.
cards/1/wrong/3: Each item exists once: an unbounded knapsack could take it twice. And a table over capacity is still too big.
cards/2/q: Decode Ways (LeetCode #91): a string of up to 100 digits, “1” → A … “26” → Z. In how many ways can it be decoded? “226” — three: 2·2·6, 22·6, 2·26. How do you solve it?
cards/2/options/0: DP like Climbing Stairs: the last “move” is one digit or two, dp[i] = dp[i − 1] + dp[i − 2] for the moves that are allowed
cards/2/options/1: Enumerate every split of the string: 100 characters isn’t much
cards/2/options/2: Greedily take two digits whenever they form a number up to 26
cards/2/explain: The last piece is one digit (if it isn’t “0”) or two (if they form 10–26), and the rest is the same problem on a prefix. It is a staircase with moves of 1 and 2, except a move isn’t always allowed. O(n) time, two variables of memory.
cards/2/wrong/1: A string of 100 digits has 2⁹⁹ splits into pieces; even with pieces of only one or two digits there are about 6·10²⁰ — the same order as the calls of the naive staircase recursion. The subproblems “how many ways for the prefix of length i” repeat, and DP counts exactly those.
cards/2/wrong/2: The question asks for the number of ways, not one way: greedy gives a single split, and on “2101” it is also wrong — “21” leaves “01”, which can’t be decoded.
cards/3/task: New coins — [2, 5], amount 11, and no coin of 1. Walk the table; the rig will stop twice and ask you to predict a cell. The rig shows unreachable sums as ∞.
cards/3/goal/asks/0/q: dp[1] = ∞, dp[2] = 1. What will dp[3] be?
cards/3/goal/asks/0/explain: Coin 2 leads from dp[1], and that is unreachable: “∞” + 1 = amount + 2 is not less than “∞” = amount + 1, so Math.Min keeps infinity. Coin 5 is larger than the sum. A 3 can’t be made from 2 and 5 — dp[3] stays ∞.
cards/3/goal/asks/1/q: dp[6] = 3, dp[9] = 3. What will dp[11] be?
cards/3/goal/asks/1/explain: Coin 2: dp[9] + 1 = 4. Coin 5: dp[6] + 1 = 4. The minimum is 4 — for example, 5 + 2 + 2 + 2. Greedy would take 5 + 5 and get stuck on the remainder 1, deciding it can’t be made; 3 coins would only be 5 + 5 + 1, and there is no coin of 1.
cards/4/q: Partition Equal Subset Sum: can the array be split into two parts with equal sums? On [1, 2, 5] the code returned true, although the answer is false. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/4/explain: The sums go up, and ok[s − x] already accounts for the number x: at x = 1 the code marks 1, 2, 3, 4 — the one is taken several times. That is the unbounded knapsack, while each number here exists once. It needs the reverse loop: for (int s = half; s >= x; s--) — then ok[s − x] hasn’t “seen” x yet.
cards/5/q: Two strings of 2·10⁴ characters each, only the LCS length is needed. How much memory does a full int table take, and what do you do about it?
cards/5/options/0: ≈ 1.6 GB; two table rows are about 160 KB, the time is the same
cards/5/options/1: ≈ 160 MB; fine, leave it as is
cards/5/options/2: ≈ 1.6 GB; switch to memoization — it stores less
cards/5/options/3: ≈ 40 KB; the table grows like m + n
cards/5/explain: (2·10⁴ + 1)² ≈ 4·10⁸ cells of 4 bytes — about 1.6 GB. A table row depends only on the previous one, so two arrays of 2·10⁴ + 1 are enough — 160 KB. The time stays O(m·n) ≈ 4·10⁸ — a few seconds, but memory is no longer a problem.
cards/5/wrong/1: 4·10⁸ cells are 4·10⁸ ints, 4 bytes each. The order is gigabytes, not hundreds of megabytes.
cards/5/wrong/2: Memoization stores the same (i, j) — up to all 4·10⁸ — plus a recursion stack up to m + n deep. No less memory.
cards/5/wrong/3: A table row grows like m + n, but the table has m·n cells.
cards/6/q: Unity: a developer console with 400 commands, names up to 20 characters. While typing, you need to show the closest ones by spelling. What do you pick?
cards/6/options/0: Edit Distance to every command on two reused rows, with a threshold k = 2–3
cards/6/options/1: LCS of the input with every command: the longer the common part, the closer
cards/6/options/2: Build a Regex from the typed string and run IsMatch over all commands
cards/6/options/3: Enumerate every string within 1–2 edits of the input and look each up in a HashSet
cards/6/explain: 400 commands · 20 · 20 is about 1.6·10⁵ cells per keystroke: on the order of a millisecond, unnoticeable while typing. Two rows kept in a field mean zero allocations; the threshold lets you drop distant names and stop a row once its minimum exceeds k.
cards/6/wrong/1: LCS doesn’t penalize extras: “spawn” is entirely inside “spawn_all_enemies_debug”, and they would look “very close”. LCS also sees a substitution typo worse than Edit Distance does.
cards/6/wrong/2: User input in a Regex risks exponential backtracking time and parse errors on characters like “*”. And Regex doesn’t forgive typos.
cards/6/wrong/3: Strings within 2 edits of a 20-character input number in the hundreds of thousands and more (replacements, insertions, deletions with 26 letters at each position), while there are only 400 commands: comparing with each is cheaper.
cards/7/q: Partition Equal Subset Sum out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/7/items/0: Clarify: are the numbers positive? what are n and the sum? may the parts be any subsets?
cards/7/items/1: Naively: enumerate subsets, 2ⁿ — impossible for n = 200
cards/7/items/2: Reduce it: we need a part with the sum total / 2; an odd sum — false at once
cards/7/items/3: The state ok[s] — can the sum s be made; each number once — sums descending
cards/7/items/4: Run [1, 5, 11, 5]: half = 11, ok[11] = true via 11 or 1 + 5 + 5
cards/7/items/6: Edge cases: a single element, an element larger than half — false at once
cards/7/explain: The reduction to “make half” is the key step, worth saying before the code. The loop direction explains that this is the 0/1 knapsack, not the unbounded one — exactly the bug from the card with the code.
cards/8/q: Which estimates are correct? Select all.
cards/8/options/0: Subsets is O(n·2ⁿ), and it can’t be faster: that many elements are in the answer itself
cards/8/options/1: Permutations is O(n·n!), for n = 11 that is already about 4·10⁸
cards/8/options/2: Edit Distance on two table rows is O(m + n) time
cards/8/options/3: LIS via tails and binary search is O(n log n)
cards/8/options/4: Coin Change is O(amount·k) time and O(amount) memory
cards/8/explain: Enumeration is optimal by the size of the answer. 11!·11 ≈ 4.4·10⁸ — at the edge of the limit. Two table rows save memory, but there are still m·n cells — the time is O(m·n). tails is n steps of O(log n). The coin table has amount cells, each trying k denominations.
